value: The two entangled obstacles of consciousness research - how to measure consciousness, and what counts as a neural correlate of it.
What are the central unresolved obstacles in empirical consciousness research, and what challenges will the field face next?

Argues that the field's two current obstacles (no agreed measure of consciousness, and contested neural correlates) are entangled because any objective or 'no-report' measure must be calibrated against introspection, and projects two future challenges: measuring consciousness 'from the outside' in non-reporting patients and artificial systems, and reconnecting empirical work to the metaphysical mind-brain question.

quote: As it will be argued below, consciousness research may face problems in the future that are currently less debated but which are logical extensions of the challenges above.
One major obstacle for consciousness research is the lacking consensus of how to optimally measure consciousness empirically.

value: measurement of consciousness and its neural correlates
quote: Historically, the attempt to “measure” consciousness has unfolded as a debate between direct and indirect approaches.

Any objective measure must be calibrated against something already known to track consciousness, and that anchor is a subjective report - so the weaknesses of introspection are re-imported into every objective method
quote: Furthermore, in order to arrive at any one particular objective method, one must have “calibrated it” to something else in order to know that this particular behavior can be considered a measure of consciousness—and not something else.

value: Objective measures work only under an unstated assumption that the threshold for a correct response coincides with the threshold for having the experience, which is what makes them fallible as measures of awareness
quote: For one thing, objective measures must assume that the “threshold” of giving a correct response is the same as the “threshold” of having a subjective experience of the same content

value: Empirical consciousness science arose less from new neuroscience technology than from an openness that let philosophical, cognitive and neuroscientific questions, methods and arguments be integrated
quote: This development was of course influenced by the technological advancements in neuroscience during those decades, but more important and fundamental was a new openness to interdisciplinary integration of research questions, methods and arguments.

value: The two obstacles are one problem: you cannot look for the correlates of something without first fixing how you will measure it
quote: This challenge clearly relates to the first as one needs to apply a measure of consciousness in order to identify its correlates.

value: An objective measure has to be calibrated against something, and the only available something is a subjective report - so the weaknesses it was designed to avoid come back in through the calibration
quote: This would typically involve associating a subjective report with a particular behavior—a process by which one would “import” all the weaknesses related to subjective reports that one tried to avoid in the first place (Overgaard, 2010 ).

value: No-report paradigms do not escape this, because associating a behavioural marker with experience in the first place requires introspection
quote: However, and as mentioned above, the only way one may associate a phenomenon as nystagmus with conscious experience is by the direct use of introspection (to establish the “correlation”) (Overgaard and Fazekas, 2016 ).

value: Objective measures also assume the threshold for a correct response coincides with the threshold for experiencing the content, which is an assumption and not a finding
quote: For one thing, objective measures must assume that the “threshold” of giving a correct response is the same as the “threshold” of having a subjective experience of the same content (Fu et al., 2008 ; Timmermans and Cleeremans, 2015 ).

value: One proposed resolution of the prefrontal-versus-occipital dispute is that both are right about different things, because there are two kinds of consciousness
quote: Block ( 2005 ) argues that there may be two neural correlates of consciousness: One relating to phenomenal consciousness (the “early” activations), and one relating to access consciousness (the “late” activations).

value: Existing evidence cannot adjudicate the metaphysical question, because it fits every position equally
quote: Existing data, however, seems to fit easily into every theoretical understanding of this problem.

value: The field's two dominant problems are not independent: neural correlates cannot be identified without first committing to a measure of consciousness, so the measurement problem is prior to the correlate problem.
quote: This challenge clearly relates to the first as one needs to apply a measure of consciousness in order to identify its correlates.

value: Objective (indirect) measures cannot escape the weaknesses of introspective report, because calibrating any objective measure requires pairing a behaviour with a subjective report in the first place.
quote: This would typically involve associating a subjective report with a particular behavior—a process by which one would “import” all the weaknesses related to subjective reports that one tried to avoid in the first place

value: So-called no-report paradigms introduce nothing that escapes introspection either, since the link between the objective marker and conscious experience can only be established by direct introspective report.
quote: the only way one may associate a phenomenon as nystagmus with conscious experience is by the direct use of introspection

value: Which measurement method is used determines which answer is obtained about the neural correlates of consciousness: some methods yield prefrontal correlates of visual consciousness, others yield occipital/parietal correlates without prefrontal involvement.
quote: Whereas this is most likely what is necessary, it is important to notice that different methods seem to generate different results, so that some methods are associated with the finding that the neural correlates of visual consciousness involve prefrontal activity, whereas other methods are associated with the finding that visual consciousness mainly involve occipital/parietal activity but not prefrontal.

value: Recent reviews favour the view that consciousness is associated with early occipital/parietal activation rather than late prefrontal activation, with late activity treated as a confound of metacognition and report.
quote: According to most recent reviews and articles, evidence is lending support toward the latter view

value: Empirical consciousness data currently do not discriminate between metaphysical positions, because existing findings can be accommodated by every theory of the mind-brain relation.
quote: Existing data, however, seems to fit easily into every theoretical understanding of this problem.

value: The next major challenge the author identifies is measuring consciousness "from the outside" - in non-responsive coma and vegetative-state patients, who have a neural system but no report, and in artificial systems, which may report but have no biological neural system.
quote: One major future challenge will be how to measure consciousness “from the outside.”

value: Despite these unsolved foundations, consciousness research already works as a discipline producing meaningful and reproducible results.
quote: Consciousness research has proven to be an actual and functioning discipline able to provide meaningful and reproducible results.
